source_read: PMC HTML (PMC3600466; the published PNAS version, 110(11):4251-4254, not an author manuscript), read in full on 2026-10-31: Abstract, all text sections, Conclusion, Methods, Acknowledgments, footnotes. Fig. 1 not inspected: the browser pane was hidden and screenshots of my tab came back blank; its content is taken from the text and caption. SI Methods (online supplement with the model details and robustness checks) not read.

claims.overstatement: None. 'Showed that ... could produce' fits a simulation that shows sufficiency under assumed parameters; the claim does not present it as evidence that SES did produce the pattern.
claims.note: Checked: no causal effect of cannabis in the model; 500 runs; trend test significant at 5% in about 50% of runs (also about 60% at 10% and about 30% at 1%). 'The main pattern' is right: what was simulated is the main table of IQ change by waves of dependence. The age-of-onset contrast was not simulated; Rogeberg lists it among the analyses that would separate the two models. Worth adding if space allows: the model assumes its key parameters, notably a temporary schooling boost for lower-SES children of about 4 IQ points (about 0.25 SD) that fades with age, and the paper reports no test of them on Dunedin data. Its one empirical pointer is Meier's own education subgroup: the 3+ group lost 0.45 SD relative to never-users with high school or less (n = 26) against about 0.24 SD with more education (n = 12). Rogeberg's 'n = 35' for the more-educated 2-wave group should be 15 (Meier Table 4: 35 − 20); my recomputation from Meier Table 4 gives 0.45, 0.24, 0.22 and 0.14. Rogeberg gives Meier's sample as 894 against 874 in Meier's Table 1, says childhood IQ was tested at 7, 9 and 11 (Meier: also 13), and says Meier adjusted only for sex and examined confounders one at a time. That last point overlooks Meier's education-adjusted model and the one multivariable model (t = −2.20). Also: the article gives significance rates only at 10%, 5% and 1%, while Meier's trend reached P < 0.0001 (t = −4.45); how often the no-effect model produced a result that strong is not reported.

anchors.locator: Comparing and Contrasting the Causal and Confounding Model, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 caption
anchors.extracted: Simulation with no causal effect of cannabis on adult IQ: (i) SES predicts cannabis exposure; (ii) lower-SES groups get a temporary IQ boost from compulsory schooling averaging 4 IQ points (about 0.25 SD) that is undone as people age out of forced environments. 500 runs of n = 875 each; the mean and 95% interval of the simulated effects are plotted against Meier et al.'s main-table estimates (given as n = 894), which fall well within the simulated range. Meier's linear-trend t test was significant in about 60% of runs at the 10% level, about 50% at 5% and about 30% at 1%.

Model built in Mathematica v6 to generate samples of similar size: three SES levels; childhood and adult IQs drawn to differ by SES; lower-SES people at higher risk of cannabis exposure at every level, with the sorting stronger at higher exposure levels. Details and robustness checks only in the SI (not read).

anchors.locator: Indications of SES Confounding in the Meier et al. Study, 1st paragraph
anchors.extracted: Own education used as a rough proxy for childhood SES, from Meier's Table 4: relative to never-users in the same education group, the 3+ dependence group lost 0.45 SD with high school or less (n = 26) against 0.24 SD with more education (n = 12); the 2-wave group 0.22 SD (n = 20) against 0.14 SD (printed n = 35, which should be 15). Caveats stated: small numbers, and less schooling could lie on the causal path. Recomputed from Meier Table 4 (subtracting the low-education subgroup from the full sample), the four values are reproduced.

anchors.locator: Who Are the Adolescent-Onset Cannabis Users?, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
anchors.extracted: Meier et al. give no table of background variables by exposure group; earlier Dunedin publications link early-onset cannabis use with poor self-control, conduct problems and risk factors correlated with low family SES; low-SES characteristics also predict dependence among people who use (a German study is cited with an odds ratio of 21.9 for young low-SES users; size in Dunedin unknown).

anchors.locator: Indications of SES Confounding in the Meier et al. Study, 2nd paragraph
anchors.extracted: Cited, second-hand: a Canadian cohort from largely middle-class families (IQ change from 9-12 to 17-20) reported no lasting effect of cannabis on IQ; a study of 1,318 people over about a decade found no effect of cannabis on cognitive decline after adjustment; a third found no effect of lifetime substance use on 1-year cognitive decline. Rogeberg notes that these studies may have had too little or too short exposure, and none tested age of onset.

anchors.locator: Confounders (subsection after Comparing and Contrasting…); Marked Differences Between Adolescent-Onset and Adult-Onset Cannabis Users; Alternative Methods for Correcting for Selection Bias
anchors.extracted: Proposed tests: a table of background traits by exposure group; one regression with childhood traits, environment, education, occupation and employment entered together (Meier's estimates are said to adjust only for sex, with confounders examined one at a time); whether adult-onset users had higher family SES and fewer risk factors; and whether exposure groups had the same IQ trajectories before use (using the repeated childhood IQ tests), or a random-growth estimator.

Meier et al.'s estimate is likely biased and the true effect could be zero; the author says it would be too strong to call the results discredited, but the method is flawed and the causal inference premature. If an effect remains after control for confounders, an alternative route is suggested: adolescent-onset heavy use linked with dropping out of school and crime, giving a non-permanent, environment-mediated effect on IQ.

key_findings.note: The finding text matches the 1st paragraph of the section. The note's values read from Fig. 1 (simulated 3+ mean about −0.29 SD, band about −0.78 to +0.26) were not checked: the browser pane was hidden and my screenshots came back blank. These values also appear in the analysis field and the 'Calibration' risk-of-bias domain.

My recomputation from Meier Table 4: more-educated never-users (242 × 0.05 + 59 × 0.03)/183 = 0.076; more-educated 3+ (38 × −0.38 + 26 × 0.48)/12 = −0.163, giving −0.24; more-educated 2-wave (35 × −0.17 + 20 × 0.25)/15 = −0.063, giving −0.14.

reporting_issues.note: 874 is checked against Meier Table 1; I did not check Meier's Fig. 1 key.

risk_of_bias.note: The editors' checklist with adapted domains, overall high, fits: the assumptions are not calibrated to Dunedin, the model was built from the confounding reading of the Meier estimates, and only the main table was compared. The 'Calibration' domain cites a Fig. 1 value I could not check, but the judgment stands without it.

interpretation_gap.note: 'Minor' is acceptable because the article hedges (results not discredited; caveats stated). But the abstract's 'likely to be overestimates' and the conclusion's 'likely biased' are probability judgments that a sufficiency simulation cannot carry. A claim should cite only 'could produce'.

missed: Rogeberg reports how often the trend test reached the 10%, 5% and 1% levels (about 60%, 50% and 30% of runs), but Meier's own trend was far stronger (t = −4.45, P < 0.0001), and the article never says how often the no-effect model produced a t that large. The simulation shows that conventional significance is common under confounding, not that a result as strong as Meier's is. Cards and claims saying the simulation 'reproduces' the Dunedin result should say so.
